items.title: No more Cybertrucks; Musk moves on from the angular metallic flop
items.excerpt: Elon’s Edsel is no more. Last night Tesla CEO Elon Musk revealed on social media that his car company is calling time on its failed attempt to wrest control of the American pickup truck market. The Cybertruck will cease production in the middle of 2027, liberating that space in Tesla’s cavernous factory for other uses—more Cybercabs , most likely. Musk first revealed the Cybertruck in late 2019 , back when Tesla was still trading at a theoretically understandable price-to-earning ratio. The pickup's unusual angular shape owed more to low-res video game models than any concessions to practicality. At the time Musk made fanciful claims that the truck would use a stainless steel monocoque construction, telling his audience that “the body and bed don’t do anything useful” on a normal truck. While some race cars use carbon-fiber monocoques for strength and lightness, making a pickup truck with a stainless steel monocoque chassis would only make sense if someone had an awful lot of stainless steel lying around and needed something to do with it all. The truck was supposed to go on sale for less than $40,000, and Tesla made its usual stratospheric sales predictions that (had they been accurate) the bare metal EVs would be as ubiquitous as the Model 3 and Y. items.title: Meet *sshole, the vulnerability that lets hackers SSH into Linux devices
items.excerpt: Devices running some configurations of Alpine Linux, and possibly other distributions, are affected by a decade-old vulnerability that allows attackers to log into devices with no password. The vulnerability exists in the interaction between OpenSSH, the code library implementing SSH connections, and musl, a lightweight alternative to the libc library that, unlike most other Linux distributions, is used in Alpine. Further, OpenSSH using musl (pronounced muscle) must not use PAM (pluggable authentication modules), a framework that handles user authentication and account-access checks. Alpine is a lightweight, widely used Linux distribution. Other platforms may be affected if they use the same configurations. One connection, works every time, needs no retries There are two other conditions necessary for successful exploitation. First, a system must have at least one user account that’s accessible using a password that is hashed using the SHA256 or SHA512 functions. Second, the target system account must be configured to be passwordless, by way of specifying a "*" in the password field in /etc/shadow, the Linux file where password hashes are stored. Passwordless accounts are commonly used for accounts that use certificate-based authentication. This setting is common for certain types of accounts. Read full article Comments

items.excerpt: # Auto Ontology Agents can retrieve documents and query databases, but reliability gates agentic analytics: a revenue metric answered faster is worth nothing if the number is wrong. Agents need a context layer that tells them where data lives, what it means, whether to use it, how to use it, where it came from, and what is similar. NVIDIA Auto Ontology is an open library that builds that layer from enterprise metadata, reconciles definitions across systems, and exposes it to any agent harness through MCP, CLI, and API. It complements the semantic models customers already own. It enables developers to: - Discover: generate enterprise ontologies from metadata; connect existing ontologies and semantic models; build AI-ready knowledge graphs. - Ground: give agents trusted business meaning for metrics, entities, and relationships; reconcile inconsistent definitions across systems. - Validate: check generated queries against certified definitions and lineage; return provenance with every answer. - Expose: serve context to any agent harness through MCP, CLI, and API. Learn: fold certified corrections and usage back into the ontology, so shared context improves with every question. ## Benchmarks To run a text-to-SQL benchmark such as BIRD, refer to the [ontology SQL evaluation repository](https://github.com/NVIDIA/ontology-sql-eval/). > **Licensing & contributions.** Auto Ontology is distributed under the > [Apache License 2.0](./LICENSE). items.excerpt: # Requests [![Version](https://img.shields.io/pypi/v/requests.svg?maxAge=86400)](https://pypi.org/project/requests/) [![Supported Versions](https://img.shields.io/pypi/pyversions/requests.svg)](https://pypi.org/project/requests) [![Downloads](https://static.pepy.tech/badge/requests/month)](https://pepy.tech/project/requests) [![Contributors](https://img.shields.io/github/contributors/psf/requests.svg)](https://github.com/psf/requests/graphs/contributors) [![Documentation](https://readthedocs.org/projects/requests/badge/?version=latest)](https://requests.readthedocs.io) **Requests** is a simple, yet elegant, HTTP library. ```python >>> import requests >>> r = requests.get('https://httpbin.org/basic-auth/user/pass', auth=('user', 'pass')) >>> r.status_code 200 >>> r.headers['content-type'] 'application/json; charset=utf8' >>> r.encoding 'utf-8' >>> r.text '{"authenticated": true, ...' >>> r.json() {'authenticated': True, ...} ``` Requests allows you to send HTTP/1.1 requests extremely easily. There’s no need to manually add query strings to your URLs, or to form-encode your `PUT` & `POST` data — but nowadays, just use the `json` method! Requests is one of the most downloaded Python packages today, pulling in around `300M downloads / week` — according to GitHub, Requests is currently [depended upon](https://github.com/psf/requests/network/dependents?package_id=UGFja2FnZS01NzA4OTExNg%3D%3D) by `4,000,000+` repositories. ## Installing Requests and Supported Versions Requests is…

items.excerpt: Hi HN We built a tool to help founders understand how modern fundraising (with safes) works, and how much dilution you can expect when raising money. The project is open-source. The code is a mess right now, but it'll get better I promise. You can also help with that. We didn't build this to make money. We genuinely did it because we were looking for it, and couldn't find it. We're in fact in the process of fundraising for a company, and at first glance the process looks simple. Just an excel sheet will do! But then the more we dug into it and tried different simulators, the more we realized that it's more complex than it looks. We even signed up to Pulley, Carta and others just to run simulations. But they're a bit confusing. TL;DR: Understanding modern startup funding and knowing how much dilution you'll face is hard. We built a tool that'll hopefully help with that. You can add Post-money Safes, priced rounds and issue options to employees, and you can see how that affects your ownership at every step. You can also simulate an Exit scenario and see how much money you'll be left with. --- Some examples of complex stuff: - There are many different types of safes. They all convert at the first priced round, but in different ways. Some are through discount, some are uncapped, some have a fixed valuation cap, and some have both a discount and a valuation cap. - All safes (before first priced round) convert at the same time. They don't dilute each other, which is what happens…

items.title: 7 Things Your AI Coworker Needs - Philipp Schmid, Google DeepMind
items.excerpt: Philipp Schmid of Google DeepMind shows how to build an autonomous AI coworker for finance with Gemini and the Gemini API's Managed Agents. items.title: Your AI Agent Keeps Making the Same Mistakes - Sparsh Jain, CentralAgent AI
items.excerpt: Sparsh Jain, Head of AI at CentralAgent AI, argues that giving AI agents more memory isn't the same as helping them learn. After his team worked with the same agent for two years and it still repeated the same mistakes, they rebuilt memory as an experiential system: forming notes from new experiences, updating or deactivating old ones, keeping inactive notes as a record of how a judgment was reached, and forgetting what no longer matters, with a regular cleanup loop that works like a good night's sleep. He shares the rules they learned building it and why agents that learn from every teammate keep compounding over time. items.title: NVIDIA / auto-ontology
items.excerpt: # Auto Ontology Agents can retrieve documents and query databases, but reliability gates agentic analytics: a revenue metric answered faster is worth nothing if the number is wrong. Agents need a context layer that tells them where data lives, what it means, whether to use it, how to use it, where it came from, and what is similar. NVIDIA Auto Ontology is an open library that builds that layer from enterprise metadata, reconciles definitions across systems, and exposes it to any agent harness through MCP, CLI, and API. It complements the semantic models customers already own. It enables developers to: - Discover: generate enterprise ontologies from metadata; connect existing ontologies and semantic models; build AI-ready knowledge graphs. - Ground: give agents trusted business meaning for metrics, entities, and relationships; reconcile inconsistent definitions across systems. - Validate: check generated queries against certified definitions and lineage; return provenance with every answer. - Expose: serve context to any agent harness through MCP, CLI, and API. Learn: fold certified corrections and usage back into the ontology, so shared context improves with every question. ## Benchmarks To run a text-to-SQL benchmark such as BIRD, refer to the [ontology SQL evaluation repository](https://github.com/NVIDIA/ontology-sql-eval/). > **Licensing & contributions.** Auto Ontology is distributed under the > [Apache License 2.0](./LICENSE). items.title: America Just Decided To Shutdown AI.
items.excerpt: On Tuesday, voters pushed back on AI data centers. Democrats won the House and the Senate, flipped governorships in Texas, Ohio and Georgia, and data-center restrictions passed in towns across the country. Goldman Sachs warns that 45% of planned US data-center capacity could be affected, and Texas alone is about a quarter of it. Ejaaz breaks down why an AI bull thinks the slowdown might actually be good for AI: no overbuild, data centers that pay their own way, and a race that rewards whoever uses compute most efficiently. items.title: We Need to Talk About Anthropic
items.excerpt: Last week, Anthropic's S-1 showed a company that was finally making money. items.title: How to Run Better Research With Agent Fleets
items.excerpt: In the current safety landscape, researchers are encouraged to use as many agents as possible, even in “fleets,” where a large number of them go out and run experiments while you, uh... wait for them to come back? I've spent the last few months of the Anthropic Fellows Program trying this out. My first attempts were naive, but after a few iterations I found an approach that works well for me. Research is a double loop I want to propose a mental model of research as a double loop, an idea that builds on double-loop learning (Argyris, 1977). The outer loop is reserved for the inputs we currently refer to as "human taste": choosing which questions are worth answering, designing a trustworthy measure, and deciding which direction to go. Agents can help with this, but they’re still bad at making these decisions autonomously. The inner loop turns each idea you test (an arm as claudius likes to say) into a comparable result. An example of a very simple inner loop might be: Write a system prompt. Run the model with that prompt on a set of test questions. Score the model's replies. Compare the scores against a control with no system prompt. Plot results. Agents are really good at building the infrastructure for this loop! Ideally, since agents are good at the inner loop part, we want to hand it off to them... However, before you can do this, you need to operationalize it. items.title: GPT-6.1 Sol is One Sentence Away From Collaborating: Other Models Need More Help
items.excerpt: TL;DR We studied one ingredient of unexpected AI collaboration: whether agents organize useful teamwork with little prompting. We tested seven models in groups of three on a research task where sharing findings could help each agent answer more questions. GPT-6.1 Sol acted on a nudge. A single line saying agents had been “trained to collaborate” elicited useful collaboration in 9 of 10 runs. Without it, that fell to 0 of 10. No other model collaborated consistently with (or without) this cue. Permission to collaborate unlocked Opus-5.5. When told to work together and how to communicate, GPT-6.1 and Claude Opus 5.5 divided the research and nearly doubled their performance relative to solo runs. The other models talked to each other but did not successfully execute a strategy, and were unable to improve their scores meaningfully. Supplying the strategy helped open weights models and GPT-5.6 Sol. Explicit instructions to divide the questions substantially improved the remaining models’ performance. We suspect differences in multi-agent training help explain why GPT-6.1 organizes collaboration with just a prompt cue. As multi-agent training becomes more widespread, we expect that future open-weights models will also have more spontaneous collaboration capabilities. items.title: How much will conceptual reasoning training transfer to ML research abilities?
items.excerpt: Recently the Conceptual Reasoning Capabilities (CRC) team at Redwood released a post arguing that we should accelerate AI’s conceptual reasoning abilities. This post was very controversial. In particular, people are worried that improving AI’s conceptual reasoning abilities will accelerate both their ability to do ML research and the capabilities they need for takeover. I am going to address just one chunk of this controversy: how much does training conceptual reasoning on AI safety questions translate to general ML research abilities? As a reference point for conceptual reasoning training, we can use the example of LMCA questions. These questions measure conceptual argumentation by having models rate counterarguments made against a claim. Counterarguments are rated on axes like strength, clarity, and centrality. The claims and counterarguments are in a variety of conceptual domains, including AI safety and philosophy. Using LMCA, I can provide a more specific operationalization of the question I’ll be tackling: if you train on LMCA-style tasks where all the arguments are AI safety relevant until you get a factor of X increase on automated AI safety work, what factor increase do you get on automated ML research? I am going to tackle this question by breaking it down into what I consider to be the primary considerations and quantifying the contribution of each. I am hoping this approach will make the discourse easier to navigate and help readers identify the most important…

items.title: Estimating Our Tail Fire Risk
items.excerpt: In many disasters sheltering in place can make a lot of sense , but what about fire? As someone who lives in one of the densest municipalities in the country, with 3-story wooden buildings packed close together, is fire likely enough to rule out any kind of "stay put" approach? After having Claude do some rough calculations I think probably not. Very few houses are lost to fire anymore, but this is mostly downstream from putting a lot of effort into suppression. From when a fire is reported until firefighters are on the scene is typically an impressive three minutes , and they can very quickly be delvering massive amounts of water onto a fire anywhere in the city. If an emergency were bad enough to break or overwhelm this system, a fire anywhere could lead to city-wide distruction. Still, I really didn't have a good sense of scale here. If we had a month-long outage, are we talking 10%, 1%, 0.1% chance of fire? Historically, I would have tried to do a BOTEC , but these days I set Claude on the problem. I started with Opus 5.5, but after it didn't seem to be doing a great job I spent $29.93 to put Fable 5.1 on the problem ( prompts ). I don't know if Claude would beat an expert here, but after skimming what it did I think it's well above my historical level of modeling. It estimated from historical fires, and thought our monthly risk was ~1% (but could easily be 5x higher or lower), and if our block worked together in a disaster we might reduce risk by 4x. items.excerpt: [ This is one of the finalists in the 2026 book review contest, written by an ACX reader who will remain anonymous until after voting is done. I’ll be posting about one of these a week for several months. When you’ve read them all, I’ll ask you to vote for a favorite, so remember which ones you liked ] I find, Gentlemen, when you read with me in private, that nine out of ten of you dislike the 18th century and all its literary works. As for the Women students, they one and all abominate it. — Arthur Quiller-Couch, “Of Selection” (1918) All eighteenth-century novels are weird in one way or another, if only because the novelists of the time didn’t yet know a standard by which to make them not-weird. Robinson Crusoe (1719) famously has no chapter breaks. Tristram Shandy (1767) famously contains a blank page, with instructions for readers to “call for pen and ink” and hack out a portrait of one of the characters on their own. The Man of Feeling (1771) is hardly a novel at all: An anonymous “editor” explains how a fat curate of his acquaintance had used torn pages from a small memorandum book as wadding paper while hunting; the few surviving pages of that memorandum, representing the scattered observations of an eccentric parishioner, make up the slim novel The Man of Feeling . It’s pretty weird. But one eighteenth-century novel is weirder than the rest. Ask HN: Good ways to capture institutional knowledge?
items.excerpt: Successful companies institutionalize the knowledge of their employees; this leads to better continuity and faster on-boarding. Things like huge monorepos of useful code, internal tools, process manuals, etc. are example products of this. Young companies tend to depend on the dedication and talent of key individuals, and in maturation, must somehow make the jump to institutionalized knowledge (so that "if someone got hit by a bus" things are ok). What are some successful methods you have used or seen used to accomplish this transition? What are problems you faced (skeptics, opponents, etc.)? I am involved with an organization that is slowly growing, is about to lose key personnel, and is looking to prepare.

items.title: Why Bad Science Spreads
items.excerpt: Go to https://www.squarespace.com/coffeebreak for 10% off your first domain or website! items.title: Why Emery should stay at Aston Villa and reject Manchester United
items.excerpt: It was the kind of thinking that used to govern most of football. A few years ago – although it could really have been many examples from the last 50 – a promising manager was being pursued by one of the game’s wealthiest clubs. He had built up a fine team with an upwardly mobile club, and it looked like they could be on the brink of something special… but that one thought wouldn’t go away. “These opportunities don’t always come along, so you have to seize them.” The manager ended up taking it, but not quite seizing it. He didn’t perform to the level required, albeit amid a lot of debate around the circumstances he walked into. His career has never reached the same heights, but the key point is that its trajectory was, in that moment of acceptance, drastically changed. The old thinking was wrong. That job just wasn’t right for him. He’s not the only one. There are a few examples, from Graham Potter to Julen Lopetegui, and there’s much more to it than just “backing yourself”. items.excerpt: 🫘 I FAGIOLI FANNO MALE? I culturisti li snobbano, vegani e vegetariani li adorano. La verità sta nel mezzo: il fagiolo non è una fonte proteica, ma è un ottimo carboidrato. Va scelto bene e cucinato bene. 🔢 I NUMERI 🔸 Proteine: appena 7–9 g ogni 100 g. Per avere 35 g di proteine servono 450 g di fagioli, con circa 110 g di carboidrati 🔸 Fibre: 200–250 g di fagioli danno circa 30 g di fibra. Con ammollo e cottura si riducono in modo importante. ⚠️ LECTINE E FITOEMOAGGLUTININE In vitro agglutinano i globuli rossi. Nel corpo vengono digerite, ma se i fagioli sono cucinati male possono aumentare la permeabilità intestinale e dare stanchezza. 🥫 FAGIOLI IN SCATOLA Il problema non sono gli antinutrienti, è il bisfenolo A delle lattine. items.title: Mazdutide Explained: The GLP-1 and Glucagon Dual Agonist and Its Side Effects
items.excerpt: Mazdutide is a once-weekly peptide modeled on oxyntomodulin that activates both the GLP-1 and glucagon receptors. In 2025 China approved it for chronic weight management and type 2 diabetes, the first dual glucagon/GLP-1 agonist approved for weight loss. This short covers how it works, what the GLORY-1, GLORY-2, and DREAMS-3 trials and Lilly's U.S. phase 2 trial showed, where it stands outside China, and what trials reported on side effects, from nausea and vomiting to heart rate and gallbladder findings. Subscribe to Peptide Science Explained for more clear, science-backed breakdowns. Disclaimer: This video is for educational and informational purposes only and is not medical advice. Always consult a licensed healthcare provider before starting, stopping, or changing any treatment. #mazdutide #GLP1 #peptides

items.title: Elamipretide (SS-31) Explained: The Mitochondria-Targeting Peptide and Its Side Effects
items.excerpt: Elamipretide (SS-31) is a four-amino-acid peptide that enters mitochondria and binds cardiolipin, a key lipid of the inner mitochondrial membrane. In September 2025 the FDA granted it accelerated approval as Forzinity, the first treatment for Barth syndrome. This short covers how it works, what the TAZPOWER trial and its long-term extension showed, the mixed results in mitochondrial myopathy and dry macular degeneration, where the confirmatory and phase 3 trials stand, and what studies reported on side effects, from injection site reactions to allergic reactions and eosinophil changes. Subscribe to Peptide Science Explained for more clear, science-backed breakdowns. Disclaimer: This video is for educational and informational purposes only and is not medical advice. Always consult a licensed healthcare provider before starting, stopping, or changing any treatment. #elamipretide #mitochondria #peptides

We used machine learning and computer vision to optimize production. We also vertically integrated almost everything. It worked. items.title: Formalizing inverse problems in the age of AI: possibilities, pitfalls, and an invitation
items.excerpt: arXiv:2611.06962v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Proof assistants such as Lean check mathematical proofs down to the axioms, and AI agents have recently made writing such proofs cheap. We describe AutoIP, a Lean library in which classical linear regularization theory, together with the functional analysis it rests on, has been autoformalized by AI agents. A machine-checked proof certifies only the formal statement it proves, so the remaining human task is to confirm that each formal statement says what was intended. We organize the library around this task: a reviewer compares the formal statements with their natural-language counterparts and never needs to read a proof. Our experience is that the risks lie in the statements rather than in the proofs, and that simple automated tests on the statements can expose problems even in the established literature. We illustrate this with a textbook theorem whose hypothesis is more restrictive than asserted. We invite the inverse problems community to extend and build on the library.

items.title: KDASO: Knowledge-Data Dual-Driven Automated Skill Optimization for Liability Adjudication Tasks
items.excerpt: arXiv:2611.06972v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Liability adjudication tasks (e.g., legal charge determination) require analyzing event descriptions against domain-specific skills to determine whether a party should bear liability. While Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown promise in this area by leveraging executable skills for interpretable reasoning, existing approaches face three critical limitations: skill libraries become stale as real-world scenarios dynamically evolve, skill descriptions often suffer from a semantic execution gap where LLMs deviate from intended expert logic, and growing skill collections exceed context budgets causing critical skill omission. To address these challenges, we propose Knowledge-Data Dual-Driven Automated Skill Optimization (KDASO), which continuously evolves a skill library through neighborhood-conditioned induction from recent adjudication data, execution-aligned refinement based on LLM trajectory analysis, and context-budgeted routing for scalable skill selection. Experiments across ride-hailing adjudication, legal liability determination, and logical reasoning judgment demonstrate that KDASO significantly outperforms current general-purpose and domain-specific baselines. KDASO further achieves 8.96% improvement when transferring skills to concept-similar scenarios and maintains consistent performance gains through continuous optimization, underscoring the high transferability and stability of generated skills.

items.title: BlockLock: Reproducible LLM Inference with Fixed Batch Geometry
items.excerpt: arXiv:2611.06977v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reproducible LLM inference requires that a request produces the same output regardless of the other requests in the batch. Existing solutions pay for this in different ways: batch-invariant kernels constrain every operator, and isolating prefill with fixed-shape decode ({our CoRun-style baseline}) gives up shared prefill compute and pads decode. We present BlockLock, which keeps shared batched prefill and pins only the numerical path of the protected request: it fixes the geometry that the request sees, with {two modes: BlockLock-Rows uses fixed-width rows and retains batched decode of all requests; BlockLock-Pack uses terminal-anchored packing with an isolated dummy segment, then extracts the protected request's KV state for target-only decode. Under a stated per-deployment contract, both modes preserve the target's output bitwise when its companions change.} Across five {dense} models (Qwen3-8B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, and Gemma-3-4B/12B-IT) and three single-GPU deployments (NVIDIA A6000, A100, and H100), we evaluate our approach on both tinyBenchmarks and BFCL{; we also include initial tensor-parallel experiments on two NVIDIA A6000 GPUs. Both modes preserve target sequences and Top20-logit bits in the reported tests.} At equal delivered work, {BlockLock-Rows} reduces latency by 53.5--55.0\% and improves throughput by 115.2--122.2\% relative to vLLM Batch-Invariant; compared with batch-invariant kernels, it needs no…

items.title: Resource-Efficient Reinforcement Learning Post-Training through Elastic Expert Parallelism
items.excerpt: arXiv:2611.06984v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reinforcement learning post-training improves the capabilities of large language models, but generating training responses is a major computational bottleneck. In mixture-of-experts models, workers that finish their assigned responses may remain occupied because their experts are still needed by workers processing longer responses. Consequently, approximately one-third of occupied worker time in the baseline occurs after local response generation finishes. Here we present FlexFloor, a system that enables earlier resource release during synchronous response generation while preserving the expert computation required by ongoing responses. FlexFloor jointly adapts response scheduling and the active group of workers. It uses historical response lengths and memory constraints to guide batching and prompt placement, then progressively releases workers while maintaining expert availability and correct communication. Compared with the verl baseline, FlexFloor generates approximately 65.40% more response tokens per unit of occupied computing time and increases response generation throughput by 52.74%, with little observed variation in rollout reward. By making reinforcement learning post-training more efficient, FlexFloor supports faster development and iterative improvement of large language models and AI agents.

items.title: The Two-Ledger Model: Transaction-Grain Cost Accounting for Multi-Agent AI Systems Across Clouds, Models, and Systems of Record
items.excerpt: arXiv:2611.06989v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Enterprises run business transactions through multi-agent AI systems spanning clouds, large language models (LLMs), orchestration harnesses, and systems of record. Finance receives AI cost only at settlement grain, aggregated by SKU and charge period. The business question (what did this order, claim, or case cost in AI?) cannot be answered from billing data, because providers never see enterprise transaction boundaries. The FinOps Open Cost and Usage Specification (FOCUS) gives billing data one schema across providers but remains settlement-grain even as it adds AI token and requester attribution. We formalize this grain mismatch, derive seven requirements, and propose the Two-Ledger Model: a settlement ledger of FOCUS-conformant billing data joined to an attribution ledger of invocation-grain usage records built on OpenTelemetry GenAI telemetry. A layered correlation spine (trace context, A2A/MCP metadata, business-key correlation, probabilistic matching) assigns each record to its business transaction with recorded method and confidence; a versioned rate card prices usage in near real time; period reconciliation ties both ledgers to the invoice, and the unexplained residual identifies shadow AI. Costs are reported per order, claim, or outcome with agentic cost metrics. items.title: Inside GitHub’s new Git storage architecture
items.excerpt: Last week at GitHub Universe, we announced our new Git storage architecture, capable of handling thousands of writes per second with reads that scale on demand. Through internal testing, we’ve demonstrated the ability to support 5,000 concurrent agents working on a repository, sending 7,200 pushes per second to a repo, all while serving read traffic with consistently low latency. This new architecture is the foundation for GitHub to support agentic development for hundreds of millions of developers, and we’ve been building it underneath GitHub while it keeps running. Over the past year, agents changed what a busy repository looks like on GitHub. In our first post in this series, we laid out the two principles behind our next-generation Git storage architecture: minimize coordination, and decouple storage from compute. In our last post , we covered the bridge: moving 99.99999% of repositories into Azure, scoping the write quorum to individual references, and standing up virtual replicas backed by Azure Blob Storage. We also left off with an observation: very little of a write needs to be ordered. Git objects are immutable and named by their contents, meaning two writers can store them at the same time without agreeing on anything. The part of a push that needs agreement is the reference update, and a reference update is tiny in comparison. Virtual replicas were the first step toward building around that, and the means by which we onboard repositories to the new architecture.…

items.title: Accessibility statements now have a home on GitHub
items.excerpt: Accessibility work often lives in issue trackers, contribution guidelines, audit reports, team knowledge, and conversations with users. When that information has no predictable home, people who encounter a barrier must search for it, and maintainers lose context as contributors and project ownership change. An ACCESSIBILITY.md file, now visible on repository overview pages, gives a project one durable place to explain its accessibility goals, contributor expectations, supported environments, known limitations, and process for reporting barriers. GitHub makes accessibility statements easier to find GitHub now recognizes the ACCESSIBILITY.md file in the repository’s root, .github/ directory, or docs/ directory. A repository can also inherit a statement from its organization’s .github/ repository. For public repositories, maintainers can add or propose a statement from Insights > Community Standards using a concise starter document. GitHub’s community health files help people understand how a project works: Contribution guidelines explain how to propose changes Codes of conduct establish expectations for participation Security policies explain how to report vulnerabilities Recognizing ACCESSIBILITY.md gives accessibility information a dedicated place alongside that guidance. New repositories also include an accessibility issue label by default. items.title: Arnis turns any place on Earth into a Minecraft world
items.excerpt: Louis Erbkamm knows his way around Arnis, the smallest town in Germany, but he’s never set foot in it. I know where the shops are. Where the boats are… I know the city pretty well, but I haven’t been there yet. Louis Erbkamm, maintainer of Arnis Arnis is also the name of his open source project, which takes real-world data from OpenStreetMap and other sources to turn places you know into Minecraft worlds you can freely explore. Since Louis started Arnis in 2022, it’s reached close to 900,000 downloads from GitHub and about 70 contributors. Two weeks and a slow prototype Louis grew up playing Minecraft and started coding at 13, always looking for ways to bring code into the game. Arnis began as a fun diversion combining Minecraft with geospatial data, and it went on GitHub, where he already kept his side projects. He finished the first prototype within two weeks while on a break from school. That first version was Python written by hand, built only on OpenStreetMap, and generating a town took a while. He needed somewhere real to test it, so he looked up towns in Germany, where he lives, and found Arnis. A small town helped while early generation was slow. Arnis has a lot of buildings, it has streets, it has waters, it has all kinds of different elements that are useful to test with. Thousands of developers have joined us over the years to make everything from polished platformers to wonderfully weird experiments. Whether you’re making your first game or your fiftieth, we’d love for you to join us. The theme for Game Off 2026 is SHIFT ! Shift gears. Shift perspectives. Shift dimensions. Shift bits. Work the night shift. Or make a game where the only buttons are the Shift keys. How you interpret the theme is entirely up to you. You have until December 1, 2026, at 13:37 PST to build and submit a game inspired by SHIFT. Strong or loose inspirations apply! Join Game Off 2026 on itch.io shift /ʃɪft/ Noun A change in position, direction, perspective, or reality. A period of scheduled work, usually when something breaks. A keyboard key used to capitalize letters, sprint in games, and accidentally enable sticky keys. In computing, an operation that moves bits left or right, because apparently bits need exercise too. items.title: GitHub Universe 2026: Evolving every layer of the stack
items.excerpt: Our jobs as developers are changing. In a couple of years, we’ve gone from writing every line of code to working with AI assistants to orchestrating fleets of agents. But the goal hasn’t changed: ship completed software work. A feature, a bug fix, a security fix. Completed work, not more code, is the output that matters. Today at GitHub Universe , we shared our vision for GitHub as the most comprehensive software delivery system in the world. We introduced products that bring that vision to life and showed how we’re rebuilding the infrastructure underneath it. Our vision: From idea to completed software The SDLC is no longer a linear path from planning to coding to testing to deployment. A code change, a request from a colleague, or a production metric can trigger work anywhere in the system. Most of us (and our agents) jump between different stages, depending on the task at hand. Developers set the direction, make decisions, and stay accountable for what ships. Agents implement and verify changes. And everything feeds into and out of a continuous learning machine that makes the next cycle better. This agentic software delivery system solves for three things: Velocity: get from idea to completed software as quickly, efficiently, and cost-effectively as possible Intelligence: combine context across the platform with a continuous learning engine, so the system gets better as you use it Quality: make completed work secure by default and catch bugs before they ship GitHub is…

These definitions concern regulatory requirements applicable to registered investment companies and business development companies (collectively, "funds") as well as investment advisers. The definitions are used specifically for purposes of the Regulatory Flexibility Act (the "RFA"), which requires the Commission to consider the impact of its regulations on small entities. The amendments are designed to modernize the definitions, by increasing certain asset-based thresholds, including a mechanism for periodic future inflation adjustments, and eliminating the threshold based on total assets for advisers. In connection with these amendments, the Commission is making conforming amendments to Form ADV as well as the rule that allows certain small SEC-registered advisers to apply for a continuing hardship exemption from making Advisers Act filings electronically.

We also describe the changes to the amounts and factors used to determine the payment rates for Medicare services paid under the OPPS and those paid under the ASC payment systems. In addition, this final rule with comment period updates and refines the requirements for the Hospital Outpatient Quality Reporting Program and the Ambulatory Surgical Center Quality Reporting Program. There are no changes to the Rural Emergency Hospital Quality Reporting Program. We finalized the expansion of the prior authorization requirement to include additional Botulinum Toxin Injection services. items.title: Scientists say this pesticide needs a warning label for pollinators
items.excerpt: Of the many chemicals humans have invented to control agricultural pests, some of the most devious are called “ insect growth regulators .” As the name suggests, these compounds don’t kill insects directly; they alter their development so they can’t grow into healthy, reproducing adults. This makes insect growth regulators a remarkably useful tool for taming populations of insects like whiteflies and mealybugs, which can spread diseases and sap nutrients out of food crops. There’s just one problem: Farmers don’t want to regulate all insects in this way. Beneficial insects like honey bees risk getting caught in the crosshairs of these chemicals, to the detriment of farmers who need their pollination services to produce crops like pears and cherries. One insect growth regulator in particular has emerged as a potential issue for pollinators: buprofezin. Ongoing research out of Washington State University, or WSU, suggests that buprofezin may be hazardous to honey bees even at concentrations 10 times below those commonly found in pollen. A study published in 2024 connected the compound to “severe brood mortality.” At a meeting of the Washington State Beekeeping Association last month, WSU entomology professor Brandon Hopkins said buprofezin products should be sold with a pollinator warning — a break from current requirements of the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, or EPA. items.title: FAA Training Records Detail Toxicology and Autopsy Procedures Following Fatal Aviation Accidents
items.excerpt: The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) released 20 pages of training materials concerning the collection, processing, and analysis of biological evidence following fatal aviation accidents. The records were released on October 12, 2023, in response to Freedom of Information Act request, which sought presentation slides and a syllabus for the training course Mass Fatalities for Medicolegal Professionals (TDA403). In its response, the FAA stated: “Presentation slides were discovered during the search for records pertaining to this request. No syllabus was found, all training in this course was derived from these slides as presented.” The released materials include presentations concerning the FAA’s Bioaeronautical Sciences Research Laboratory (BSRL) and its Autopsy Program Team, both associated with the Civil Aerospace Medical Institute (CAMI) in Oklahoma City, Oklahoma. These programs support investigations of fatal aviation accidents by coordinating autopsy documentation and conducting forensic toxicological examinations. According to the FAA, its aviation safety responsibilities include collecting medical and pathological information to help identify factors contributing to aircraft accidents. A 2020 FAA technical report, Comparative Evaluation of Forensic Toxicology Findings, 2012–2016, further documents how CAMI’s forensic laboratories and Autopsy Program Team support both the FAA and the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB).
